questions.question: When approaching an intersection, you should:

options.text: Assume other drivers see you, especially if they make eye contact.
Never assume other drivers see you.
Stay focused on moving through the intersection.
Speed up to make others notice you.

questions.correctAnswerText: Never assume other drivers see you.
questions.explanation: Do not assume other drivers see you, even if they look at you. Drivers often look directly at motorcycles and still miss them. Always slow down when approaching an intersection.

questions.question: When riding at night compared to riding during the day, a motorcycle operator should do all of the following except:

options.text: Ride more slowly.
Allow more space between their motorcycle and other vehicles.
Use their high beam whenever possible.
Tailgate other vehicles.

questions.correctAnswerText: Tailgate other vehicles.
questions.explanation: To avoid crashes when riding at night, slow down and increase your following distance. Use the lights of vehicles ahead to see the road better. Adjust your lane position as needed, especially at night.

questions.question: Which of the following will protect your eyes from the wind?

options.text: Goggles
Windshield
Sunglasses
Eyeglasses

questions.correctAnswerText: Goggles
questions.explanation: Goggles and face shields protect your eyes from wind. Windshields, eyeglasses, and sunglasses do not provide enough protection.

questions.question: Use your mirrors when stopped at an intersection to:

options.text: See if vehicles parked on the sides of the street are entering traffic.
Look for vehicles changing lanes.
Watch for vehicles behind you that may not be slowing down.
See if someone is planning to turn behind you.

questions.correctAnswerText: Watch for vehicles behind you that may not be slowing down.
questions.explanation: When stopped at an intersection, use your mirrors to check for cars approaching from behind. Drivers may not notice you until they are too close, so you need to be ready to react.

questions.question: When approaching a blind intersection with a stop sign, riders should:

options.text: Stop at the stop sign then proceed through the intersection.
Ignore the stop sign and move forward to get a better look.
Stop at the stop sign before moving forward to improve their view of cross traffic.
Proceed through the intersection without stopping.

questions.correctAnswerText: Stop at the stop sign before moving forward to improve their view of cross traffic.
questions.explanation: Stop at the stop line or sign first. Then edge forward slowly and stop again just before the cross traffic lane. Lean forward and look around buildings, parked cars, or bushes to check for traffic. Keep your front wheel out of the crossroad while looking.

questions.question: Your lane position should:

options.text: Avoid other road users' blind spots.
Provide a good view of the shoulder.
Provide a poor view of road hazards.
Invite others to share your lane.

questions.correctAnswerText: Avoid other road users' blind spots.
questions.explanation: Choose a lane position that helps you see others and helps them see you. Do not stay in another driver's blind spot for long.

questions.question: A motorcycle with a sidecar:

options.text: Cannot tip over.
Can tip over if making a turn too fast.
Is designed to take corners at any speed.
Should not be used for loading items.

questions.correctAnswerText: Can tip over if making a turn too fast.
questions.explanation: Even with three wheels on the ground, a sidecar can tip over if you turn too sharply or go too fast around a corner.

questions.question: When riding in rain or fog, you should:

options.text: Use your high beam headlight.
Use your low beam headlight.
Not use your headlight.
Alternate between your headlight's low and high beam settings.

questions.correctAnswerText: Use your low beam headlight.
questions.explanation: Use your low beam headlight in snow, rain, or fog. A high beam reflects off these conditions and makes it harder to see.

questions.question: An advantage to keeping a cushion of space between your motorcycle and other vehicles is that:

options.text: You can pass danger more quickly.
You will have a more narrow view of the road so you can stay focused.
You will have more time to react to the movements of others.
You can more easily follow the path of the next vehicle.

questions.correctAnswerText: You will have more time to react to the movements of others.
questions.explanation: Keeping space between your motorcycle and other vehicles gives you a clearer view of hazards, more time to react, and more room to maneuver.

questions.question: Motorcycle riders should not rely only on their mirrors to see what's around them because:

options.text: Motorcycle mirrors are smaller than the mirrors on other vehicles, so you can't see as much.
Motorcycles, like cars, have blind spots.
Mirrors are never accurate.
Mirrors take your eyes off the road in front of you and they should not be used.

questions.correctAnswerText: Motorcycles, like cars, have blind spots.
questions.explanation: Motorcycles have blind spots just like other vehicles. You cannot rely only on mirrors to see what is behind you. Check your blind spots by turning your head regularly.

questions.question: A windshield:

options.text: Is a good substitute for a face shield.
Does not completely protect your eyes from the wind.
Is required on all motorcycles.
Should be used on windy days.

questions.correctAnswerText: Does not completely protect your eyes from the wind.
questions.explanation: A windshield does not protect your eyes as well as goggles or a face shield. You still need eye protection when riding.

questions.question: The gear shift lever is located:

options.text: In front of the left footrest.
In front of the right footrest.
Behind the left footrest.
Behind the right footrest.

questions.correctAnswerText: In front of the left footrest.
questions.explanation: The gear shift lever is in front of the left footrest. Use your left foot to operate it. Push up with your foot to shift to a higher gear. Push down to shift to a lower gear.

questions.question: A potential danger of braking too hard is:

options.text: Losing traction on one or both wheels.
Coming to a complete stop before you expect to.
Popping a tire.
Taking too long to stop.

questions.correctAnswerText: Losing traction on one or both wheels.
questions.explanation: Braking too hard can cause you to lose grip on the road and crash.

questions.question: Passengers should:

options.text: Lean with the operator.
Never come into contact with the operator.
Sit as far back on their seat as possible.
Hold onto their seat.

questions.correctAnswerText: Lean with the operator.
questions.explanation: Tell your passenger to lean with you during turns and curves. They should hold onto your waist, hips, or belt.

questions.question: For routine braking:

options.text: You should only use the front brake.
You should only use the rear brake.
You should alternate between the front and rear brakes to maximize the life of the brakes.
You should always use both the front and rear brakes at the same time.

questions.correctAnswerText: You should always use both the front and rear brakes at the same time.
questions.explanation: Always use both brakes every time you slow down or stop.

questions.question: In a normal turn:

options.text: The motorcycle and rider should lean together.
The motorcycle and rider should lean in opposite directions.
The motorcycle should lean, but the rider should not.
The rider should lean, but the motorcycle should not.

questions.correctAnswerText: The motorcycle and rider should lean together.
questions.explanation: During normal turns, the motorcycle and rider lean at the same angle. In slow, tight turns, only the motorcycle leans while the rider stays upright.

questions.question: When riding downhill or shifting into first gear, you may need to:

options.text: Use your brakes to slow down before downshifting safely.
Speed up before downshifting safely.
Swerve to the left.
Flash your brakes to ensure that drivers behind you know you are downshifting.

questions.correctAnswerText: Use your brakes to slow down before downshifting safely.
questions.explanation: Slow down with your brakes before shifting to a lower gear. Downshifting too fast can cause the motorcycle to jerk and the rear wheel to skid.

questions.question: Which type of sign is yellow with black lettering or symbols?

options.text: Warning
Service
Regulatory
Speed limit

questions.correctAnswerText: Warning
questions.explanation: Warning signs are yellow with black lettering or symbols. They tell you about dangerous road conditions ahead.

questions.question: Before carrying a passenger in traffic for the first time, you should:

options.text: Read books about carrying passengers.
Practice riding on an empty road.
Flash your lights so others can see you.
Practice riding on the shoulder of a road.

questions.correctAnswerText: Practice riding on an empty road.
questions.explanation: Before carrying a passenger in traffic, practice on a quiet road first. This helps you get used to how your motorcycle handles with extra weight.

questions.question: Maximum straight-line braking is done by:

options.text: Using only the rear brake.
Using only the front brake.
Using both the front and rear brakes without locking either wheel.
Using both the front and rear brakes while locking the rear wheel.

questions.correctAnswerText: Using both the front and rear brakes without locking either wheel.
questions.explanation: To stop in the shortest distance on a straight road, use both brakes. Do not lock either brake.

questions.question: If the front wheel locks, what should you do?

options.text: Keep holding the brake until the skid stops.
Release the front brake and do not use it.
Release the front brake and squeeze it again quickly.
Release the front brake right away and apply it smoothly again.

questions.correctAnswerText: Release the front brake right away and apply it smoothly again.
questions.explanation: If your front wheel locks, release the front brake immediately. Then apply the brake smoothly.

questions.question: Why do riders move into another lane while taking a curve?

options.text: Entering the turn too fast.
Lanes that are too narrow.
Not knowing how to steer.
Lanes that are too wide.

questions.correctAnswerText: Entering the turn too fast.
questions.explanation: Taking a curve too fast can cause you to move into another lane or leave the road.

questions.question: What does an experienced rider do?

options.text: Changes lane position as road and traffic conditions change.
Stays in one spot in the lane at all times.
Weaves within the lane to stay visible.
Rides only on the oily part of the lane.

questions.correctAnswerText: Changes lane position as road and traffic conditions change.
questions.explanation: A motorcycle rider has three lane positions to choose from. Pick the safest position based on current road and traffic conditions.

questions.question: When braking, what should you do?

options.text: Always use both brakes.
Only use the front brake.
Only use the rear brake on wet pavement.
Only use the rear brake.

questions.correctAnswerText: Always use both brakes.
questions.explanation: Use both brakes every time you slow down or stop, no matter what the road conditions are.

questions.question: How can you prevent fatigue on a long trip?

options.text: Ride as far as possible without stopping to reach your destination faster.
Take artificial stimulants.
Dress warmly to protect yourself from wind and cold.
Do not set daily riding limits.

questions.correctAnswerText: Dress warmly to protect yourself from wind and cold.
questions.explanation: Protect yourself from tiring weather like wind and cold by dressing properly. Limit riding to about six hours per day and take a break every two hours. Avoid artificial stimulants because you may feel very tired when they wear off.
